name: Galvin Seeks Help from Dr. Gruber at His Home
description: Galvin steps out of a taxi and hurries up the steps of a brownstone. He peers through the side window, sees no light inside, and grabs the brass knocker, pounding on the door. There is no answer. He pounds again. Still nothing. He stands on the steps, exhausted, then slowly begins to walk back down. Behind him, the door opens. He turns. A middle-aged Black woman in livery stands in the doorway. She asks what he wants. Galvin says he is looking for Dr. Gruber. The maid tells him Dr. Gruber is not in. Galvin explains he had an appointment at the office and may have gotten the time wrong—they were supposed to meet. The maid repeats that the doctor is not in. Galvin asks where he is. The maid hesitates, then says Dr. Halpern is handling his patients. Galvin steps up toward the door, insisting he must speak to Dr. Gruber. He says his wife’s prescription has run out and he needs to call the doctor. The maid pauses, then tells him he can’t reach Dr. Gruber—he’s on an island in the Caribbean with no phone. He won’t be back for a week. She offers Dr. Halpern’s number. Galvin doesn’t respond. He turns away from the door, still holding a box of cigars, and walks down the steps.

name: Galvin and Laura Share Drinks and a Late-Night Conversation
description: Galvin and Laura sit in a dimly lit booth, the remnants of their dinner scattered across the table, empty glasses and cigarette smoke curling into the air. They lean toward each other, speaking intently, their voices low and thick with drink. Galvin raises a hand to signal the bartender, pointing to their glasses, and a moment later, fresh drinks arrive. He talks about the weak needing someone to fight for them, about courts and juries, about the faint hope that justice might be possible. Laura listens, her eyes on his, asking if the people will actually get justice. Galvin pauses, then says they might—that’s the point. He tells her about having to choose twelve jurors from a hundred faces, each one carrying doubt in their expression but a quiet hope in their heart. 'Maybe,' he says. 'Maybe I can do something right.' Laura looks at him and asks if that’s what he’s going to do. He meets her gaze and says, 'That’s what I’m going to try to do.'

He calls over to the bartender, signaling for another round. Laura asks if the people will actually get justice. Galvin says they might, and that’s the point. He explains that the next day he’ll have to pick a jury, going through a hundred people to find twelve. He says he can see it on their faces—they think the whole thing is a sham—but deep down, they’re hoping, just maybe, that something real can happen. Laura looks at him and asks if that’s what he’s going to do. Galvin pauses, then says that’s what he’s going to try to do.

name: Galvin and Sally Discuss the Medical Malpractice Case
description: Galvin sits at his secretary's desk with Sally Doneghy across from him by the coffee table. He tells her the case is not just good—it's very good. A healthy young woman went into the hospital to deliver her third child and was given the wrong anesthetic. Sally interrupts, saying she and her husband Dick love the woman deeply. Galvin acknowledges this. Sally says the woman no longer recognizes visitors. Galvin confirms he has seen her. Sally speaks of how beautiful the woman once was, and how her husband left, taking the children. She says the facility where the woman is kept, the Patriot Home for Chronic Care in Arlington, demands fifty thousand dollars as an endowment for her care. She doesn't want to leave her, but her doctor advised her to move out West, which is when they filed in court. They never wanted to sue. Galvin listens and says he understands. Sally explains that Dick has a job opportunity in Tucson and was called to come out. She insists he is a good man trying to do what's right. The door opens and Dick Doneghy enters. Sally introduces him. Galvin stands, shakes his hand, and invites them both to sit. He apologizes for meeting in the outer office, explaining his own is filled with papers for a case in two days. He repeats to Dick that they have a very strong case. Sally adds that Galvin has already seen the woman at Northern Care. Galvin says he has reached out to medical experts, though it is difficult to find doctors willing to testify against other doctors. Dick mentions the Archdiocese called, asking who their attorney was, since the case is coming to trial. Galvin says he doubts it will go to trial. Dick says they didn't want it to come to this. Sally says they just can't do it anymore. After a pause, she adds that this is their chance to get away. Galvin assures them he will make sure they get that chance. Dick asks what it will cost. Galvin explains it's on a contingency basis—he takes one-third of any settlement, which is the usual arrangement.

description: Mickey Morrissey unlocks the door to Galvin's dark anteroom and steps inside, looking around. Mickey walks into the office and stands over Galvin. He tells him sharply to get up. When Galvin stirs and swings his legs off the couch, he reaches for the glass and takes a drink. Mickey demands to know what he is doing, gesturing at the mess in the room. He says Sally Doneghy called him, furious that Galvin hasn’t met with her or prepared for a case they were counting on. Galvin asks who she is. Mickey reminds him he sent a letter eighteen months ago, arranged a doctor to speak with him, and has been doing all the work. He says the clients are arriving the next day and Galvin hasn’t even looked at the file. Galvin pours another drink. Mickey steps forward, knocks the glass from his hand, and slaps him in the face several times. He tells Galvin he’s done, that nothing is changing, and he can’t keep enabling him. He says the case could have taken care of Galvin, but it’s over. He walks out and slams the door. Galvin sits on the couch, looks around, then reaches for a pack of Luckies on the side table. His hand trembles as he takes a cigarette. The table also holds a pile of loose change, a small rosary, and a wedding ring.

name: Alito Briefs the Bishop on Galvin's Past
description: In a finely furnished office with French windows overlooking Boston Common, Joseph Alito stands near the fireplace, holding a leather folder filled with news clippings and notes. He reads aloud, recounting Frank Galvin's history. A yellowed clipping shows Galvin in his thirties, well-dressed and standing beside Patricia Harrington, a patrician woman in her twenties, smiling at the camera beneath a headline announcing their engagement. Alito notes Galvin’s graduation from B.U. Law, second in his class, his role as editor of the Law Review, and his partnership at Stearns, Harrington, Pierce in 1960. He mentions Galvin’s marriage to Patricia Harrington that same year. Another clipping appears—Galvin at around forty-five, looking dazed, being led into jail under a headline accusing him of jury tampering. Alito clarifies that Galvin was never indicted. He explains that Galvin resigned from the firm in 1969 over the Lillibridge case, divorced Patricia in 1970, and continued working with Michael Morrissey until Morrissey’s retirement in 1978. Since then, Galvin practiced alone, losing all four of his cases in the Circuit Court. Alito adds that Galvin now drinks. Bishop Brophy, seated on a leather couch, listens in silence. When Alito finishes, Brophy asks about the current case. Alito calls it a nuisance suit, a bid for six hundred thousand dollars, and insists Galvin is too afraid to go to trial. Brophy states he wants to settle, to keep the Archdiocese out of the matter, and intends to make the offer himself. Alito agrees, advising to keep the amount low, and mentions he has consulted Ed Concannon, who recommends maintaining a posture of preparing for trial. As Alito moves to leave, Brophy asks one final question: if they were to go to trial, would they win? Alito pauses, then says yes. He picks up his folder from the desk, the clipping of Galvin being taken into custody still visible inside, and snaps it shut.
